blocks.en: Professor: Dr. Wayne Cook | Director: Dr. Ted Rogers
blocks.es_reference: Profesor: Dr. Wayne Cook | Director: Dr. Ted Rogers

blocks.en: "Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and lean not on your own understanding." — Proverbs 3:5 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "Fíate de Jehová de todo tu corazón, y no estribes en tu propia prudencia." — Proverbios 3:5 (RVG)

blocks.en: 1. New Wineskins of Faith
blocks.es_reference: 1. Odres Nuevos de Fe

blocks.en: Proverbs 3:5-6 (NKJV): "Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and lean not on your own understanding; in all your ways acknowledge Him, and He shall direct your paths."
blocks.es_reference: Proverbios 3:5-6 (RVG): "Fíate de Jehová de todo tu corazón, y no estribes en tu propia prudencia. Reconócelo en todos tus caminos, y él enderezará tus veredas."

blocks.en: When Jesus said no one pours new wine into old wineskins, He was describing the radical new life He brings. New wine ferments and expands, and old, brittle skins burst under the pressure; only new wineskins can stretch to hold it. In the same way, Jesus calls His disciples into a faith that stretches us beyond what feels safe or comfortable. He calls us to a radical trust — the kind that does not collapse under storms, worries, or uncertainty.
blocks.es_reference: Cuando Jesús dijo que nadie echa vino nuevo en odres viejos, estaba describiendo la vida nueva y radical que Él trae. El vino nuevo fermenta y se expande, y los odres viejos y frágiles revientan bajo la presión; solo los odres nuevos pueden estirarse para contenerlo. De la misma manera, Jesús llama a sus discípulos a una fe que nos estira más allá de lo que se siente seguro o cómodo. Nos llama a una confianza radical — la que no se derrumba bajo las tormentas, las preocupaciones, ni la incertidumbre.

blocks.en: Proverbs sets the terms of that trust. We are to trust the LORD with all our heart, not a cautious portion of it, and specifically told to stop leaning on our own understanding — the hard part, since our understanding is exactly what we reach for when life turns frightening. Radical trust means letting go of the handrail of our own calculations and resting our whole weight on God. In this unit we watch that trust be stretched in three directions: trusting the Lord over storms, over worry, and over what we cannot yet see.
blocks.es_reference: Proverbios fija los términos de esa confianza. Hemos de confiar en Jehová de todo nuestro corazón, no con una porción cautelosa de él, y se nos dice específicamente que dejemos de estribar en nuestra propia prudencia — la parte difícil, ya que nuestra prudencia es justo lo que buscamos cuando la vida se vuelve temible. La confianza radical significa soltar el pasamanos de nuestros propios cálculos y descansar todo nuestro peso en Dios. En esta unidad vemos esa confianza estirada en tres direcciones: confiar en el Señor sobre las tormentas, sobre la preocupación, y sobre lo que aún no podemos ver.

blocks.en: 2. The Lord Over Storms
blocks.es_reference: 2. El Señor Sobre las Tormentas

blocks.en: Mark 4:39-40 (NKJV): "Then He arose and rebuked the wind, and said to the sea, 'Peace, be still!' And the wind ceased and there was a great calm. But He said to them, 'Why are you so fearful? How is it that you have no faith?'"
blocks.es_reference: Marcos 4:39-40 (RVG): "Y levantándose, reprendió al viento, y dijo al mar: Calla, enmudece. Y cesó el viento, y fue hecha grande bonanza. Y a ellos dijo: ¿Por qué estáis así amedrentados? ¿Cómo es que no tenéis fe?"

blocks.en: Jesus asked His disciples to cross the Sea of Galilee, and as they sailed a violent storm broke out, so fierce that the boat began filling with water. These were seasoned fishermen, yet the waves terrified them — and where was Jesus? Asleep in the stern, resting on a cushion. They shook Him awake: "Teacher, do You not care that we are perishing?" He stood, rebuked the wind, and said to the waves, "Peace, be still." The storm stopped at once, and they whispered in astonishment, "Who can this be, that even the wind and the sea obey Him?"
blocks.es_reference: Jesús pidió a sus discípulos cruzar el mar de Galilea, y mientras navegaban estalló una violenta tormenta, tan feroz que la barca empezó a llenarse de agua. Eran pescadores experimentados, pero las olas los aterrorizaron — ¿y dónde estaba Jesús? Dormido en la popa, descansando sobre un cabezal. Lo despertaron sacudiéndolo: "Maestro, ¿no tienes cuidado que perecemos?" Se levantó, reprendió al viento, y dijo a las olas: "Calla, enmudece." La tormenta cesó al instante, y susurraron asombrados: "¿Quién es éste, que aun el viento y el mar le obedecen?"

blocks.en: The lesson is not that storms will never come. The lesson is that the Lord of the storm is in the boat with you. Radical trust knows that His presence is greater than any wave. Notice that His question to them was not "why did the storm come?" but "how is it that you have no faith?" The danger was real, but so was the sleeping Savior beside them — and faith is simply remembering who is in the boat.
blocks.es_reference: La lección no es que las tormentas nunca vendrán. La lección es que el Señor de la tormenta está en la barca contigo. La confianza radical sabe que su presencia es mayor que cualquier ola. Note que su pregunta a ellos no fue "¿por qué vino la tormenta?" sino "¿cómo es que no tenéis fe?" El peligro era real, pero también lo era el Salvador dormido junto a ellos — y la fe es sencillamente recordar quién está en la barca.

blocks.en: Elisabeth Elliot: In 1956 five young missionaries were speared to death in Ecuador while trying to reach the Huaorani tribe. Jim Elliot's wife, Elisabeth, just twenty-nine with a baby daughter, was left a widow. She could have surrendered to bitterness and fear. Instead she trusted the Lord of the storm, and two years later went to live among the very tribe that had killed her husband, showing them the love of Christ. In time many Huaorani came to faith — including some of the men who had held the spears.
blocks.es_reference: Elisabeth Elliot: En 1956 cinco jóvenes misioneros fueron asesinados a lanzazos en Ecuador al tratar de alcanzar a la tribu huaorani. La esposa de Jim Elliot, Elisabeth, de apenas veintinueve años y con una hija bebé, quedó viuda. Pudo haberse entregado a la amargura y el miedo. En cambio confió en el Señor de la tormenta, y dos años después fue a vivir entre la misma tribu que había matado a su esposo, mostrándoles el amor de Cristo. Con el tiempo muchos huaorani vinieron a la fe — incluidos algunos de los hombres que habían empuñado las lanzas.

blocks.en: 3. Presence Over Outcome
blocks.es_reference: 3. La Presencia Por Encima del Resultado

blocks.en: Elisabeth Elliot's story teaches us what trust actually rests on, because her storm was never calmed in the way she might have wished. Her husband was not given back to her. And yet the same Jesus who stilled the Sea of Galilee was unmistakably with her in the deeper storm, and ruled over it to bring a harvest she could never have engineered. Faith does not always stop the storm; what it always does is anchor us to the Savior who rules over it.
blocks.es_reference: La historia de Elisabeth Elliot nos enseña en qué descansa de veras la confianza, porque su tormenta nunca fue calmada como ella habría deseado. Su esposo no le fue devuelto. Y sin embargo el mismo Jesús que aquietó el mar de Galilea estuvo inconfundiblemente con ella en la tormenta más honda, y reinó sobre ella para traer una cosecha que ella jamás habría podido producir. La fe no siempre detiene la tormenta; lo que siempre hace es anclarnos al Salvador que reina sobre ella.

blocks.en: This corrects a shallow idea of trust. We often assume trusting God means He will give us the calm we ask for — the healing, the rescue, the restored situation. But the disciples' deepest need in the boat was not calmer water; it was to know who was with them. You may not be able to calm your storm, but you can rest in the One who commands it. So the first instinct of radical trust, when the wind rises, is to pray first rather than panic first — turning at once to the One asleep in the stern, who is in fact Lord of the wind and the waves.
blocks.es_reference: Esto corrige una idea superficial de la confianza. A menudo suponemos que confiar en Dios significa que Él nos dará la calma que pedimos — la sanidad, el rescate, la situación restaurada. Pero la necesidad más honda de los discípulos en la barca no era agua más calmada; era saber quién estaba con ellos. Quizá no puedas calmar tu tormenta, pero puedes descansar en Aquel que la manda. Así que el primer instinto de la confianza radical, cuando se levanta el viento, es orar primero en vez de entrar en pánico primero — volverse de inmediato a Aquel dormido en la popa, que es de hecho el Señor del viento y de las olas.

blocks.en: 4. The Lord Over Worry
blocks.es_reference: 4. El Señor Sobre la Preocupación

blocks.en: Matthew 6:31-33 (NKJV): "Therefore do not worry, saying, 'What shall we eat?' or 'What shall we drink?'... For your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things. But seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you."
blocks.es_reference: Mateo 6:31-33 (RVG): "No os afanéis, pues, diciendo: ¿Qué comeremos, o qué beberemos...? Porque vuestro Padre celestial sabe que de todas estas cosas tenéis necesidad. Mas buscad primeramente el reino de Dios y su justicia, y todas estas cosas os serán añadidas."

blocks.en: From the dramatic storm Jesus turns to the quiet, daily storm of anxiety: food, drink, clothing, the ordinary cares that keep us awake at night. "Do not worry about your life," He says, and points to the birds of the air, which neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, yet the heavenly Father feeds them. He points to the lilies of the field, which neither toil nor spin, yet not even Solomon in all his glory was arrayed like one of them. If God so clothes the grass, will He not much more clothe you?
blocks.es_reference: De la dramática tormenta Jesús se vuelve a la tormenta callada y diaria de la ansiedad: comida, bebida, vestido, los cuidados ordinarios que nos mantienen despiertos de noche. "No os afanéis por vuestra vida," dice, y señala las aves del cielo, que no siembran ni siegan ni recogen en graneros, y sin embargo el Padre celestial las alimenta. Señala los lirios del campo, que no trabajan ni hilan, y sin embargo ni aun Salomón con toda su gloria fue vestido así como uno de ellos. Si Dios viste así a la hierba, ¿no os vestirá mucho más a vosotros?

blocks.en: Then He asks the question that exposes worry for what it is: "which of you by worrying can add one cubit to his stature?" Worry accomplishes nothing; it changes no outcome and adds not a single hour to our lives. It is, in the end, a failure to reckon with the Father's care. So Jesus gives the antidote: "seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you." Radical trust surrenders anxiety to the Father who already knows exactly what we need before we ask.
blocks.es_reference: Luego hace la pregunta que desenmascara la preocupación: "¿quién de vosotros podrá, afanándose, añadir a su estatura un codo?" La preocupación no logra nada; no cambia ningún resultado y no añade una sola hora a nuestra vida. Es, al final, una falta de contar con el cuidado del Padre. Así que Jesús da el antídoto: "buscad primeramente el reino de Dios y su justicia, y todas estas cosas os serán añadidas." La confianza radical entrega la ansiedad al Padre que ya sabe exactamente lo que necesitamos antes de pedir.

blocks.en: 5. From "What If?" to "Even If"
blocks.es_reference: 5. De "¿Qué Tal Si?" a "Aun Si"

blocks.en: The practical shape of trusting God over worry is a change of vocabulary in the heart. Anxiety speaks the language of "what if?" — what if the paycheck runs out, what if the diagnosis is bad, what if I cannot provide? Faith answers in the language of "even if." Even if the paycheck is small, even if the refrigerator is empty, even if the future is uncertain — God is still faithful, and He still knows what I need. The "what if" multiplies fears that may never arrive; the "even if" rests on a God who is certain to remain good.
blocks.es_reference: La forma práctica de confiar en Dios sobre la preocupación es un cambio de vocabulario en el corazón. La ansiedad habla el idioma del "¿qué tal si?" — qué tal si se acaba el sueldo, qué tal si el diagnóstico es malo, qué tal si no puedo proveer. La fe responde en el idioma del "aun si." Aun si el sueldo es pequeño, aun si el refrigerador está vacío, aun si el futuro es incierto — Dios sigue siendo fiel, y sigue sabiendo lo que necesito. El "qué tal si" multiplica temores que tal vez nunca lleguen; el "aun si" descansa en un Dios que con certeza permanecerá bueno.

blocks.en: Empty fridge, full faith: Believers have testified to this again and again in hard economic seasons. Picture a single mother in a deep recession, recently out of work, bills piling up, the refrigerator nearly empty, lying awake over how she will feed her children. One night she breaks down in the kitchen and prays, "Lord, I don't know how we'll eat tomorrow, but You promised to care for us, and I trust You." The next morning a friend from church arrives with bags of groceries: "I couldn't sleep last night — I felt God telling me you needed this." Such testimonies, repeated in countless lives, make one point: God shows us we need not live in fear, because He knows what we need before we ask.
blocks.es_reference: Refrigerador vacío, fe llena: Los creyentes han dado testimonio de esto una y otra vez en temporadas económicas duras. Imagine a una madre soltera en una profunda recesión, recién sin trabajo, las cuentas amontonándose, el refrigerador casi vacío, desvelada por cómo alimentará a sus hijos. Una noche se quiebra en la cocina y ora: "Señor, no sé cómo comeremos mañana, pero prometiste cuidarnos, y confío en Ti." A la mañana siguiente una amiga de la iglesia llega con bolsas de comestibles: "No pude dormir anoche — sentí que Dios me decía que necesitabas esto." Tales testimonios, repetidos en incontables vidas, exponen un punto: Dios nos muestra que no tenemos que vivir en temor, porque Él sabe lo que necesitamos antes de pedir.

blocks.en: So the disciplines of trust are simple but daily: surrender each worry to the Lord, who carries it better than we do; seek first the kingdom, choosing obedience, generosity, and worship over anxiety; and begin each day thanking God for His provision even before we see it arrive, because gratitude is faith remembering that the Father has never failed.
blocks.es_reference: Así que las disciplinas de la confianza son sencillas pero diarias: entrega cada preocupación al Señor, que la lleva mejor que nosotros; busca primero el reino, eligiendo la obediencia, la generosidad y la adoración por encima de la ansiedad; y comienza cada día agradeciendo a Dios por su provisión aun antes de verla llegar, porque la gratitud es la fe que recuerda que el Padre nunca ha fallado.

blocks.en: 6. The Lord of Sight
blocks.es_reference: 6. El Señor de la Vista

blocks.en: Hebrews 11:8 (NKJV): "By faith Abraham obeyed when he was called to go out to the place which he would receive as an inheritance. And he went out, not knowing where he was going."
blocks.es_reference: Hebreos 11:8 (RVG): "Por la fe Abraham, siendo llamado, obedeció para salir al lugar que había de recibir por herencia; y salió sin saber a dónde iba."

blocks.en: The third stretching of trust concerns the future we cannot see. Abraham was called to leave his home for a land he had never laid eyes on, and he went out not knowing where he was going. Romans 4 tells us he believed God's promise of a son even when his body and Sarah's were as good as dead. This is radical trust at its furthest reach: to obey before the map is clear, to stake everything on the promise of God rather than on the evidence of our eyes.
blocks.es_reference: El tercer estiramiento de la confianza concierne al futuro que no podemos ver. Abraham fue llamado a dejar su hogar por una tierra que nunca había visto, y salió sin saber a dónde iba. Romanos 4 nos dice que creyó la promesa de Dios de un hijo aun cuando su cuerpo y el de Sara estaban como muertos. Ésta es la confianza radical en su alcance más extremo: obedecer antes de que el mapa esté claro, apostarlo todo a la promesa de Dios en vez de a la evidencia de nuestros ojos.

blocks.en: Adoniram Judson: In 1812 Adoniram and Ann Judson sailed from Boston to Burma as among the first American missionaries, leaving family and security for a dangerous unknown. The work was agonizingly slow — seven years before the first convert. Disease struck repeatedly; they buried children. Adoniram was imprisoned nearly two years in filthy conditions, while Ann risked her life daily to bring him food until her own health failed and she died young. From the outside it looked like failure. Yet in his darkest hour Adoniram wrote, "the future is as bright as the promises of God." Today more than four million Christians in Myanmar trace their heritage to the Judsons' faithfulness.
blocks.es_reference: Adoniram Judson: En 1812 Adoniram y Ann Judson zarparon de Boston a Birmania como de los primeros misioneros estadounidenses, dejando familia y seguridad por un desconocido peligroso. La obra fue angustiosamente lenta — siete años antes del primer convertido. La enfermedad golpeó repetidamente; enterraron hijos. Adoniram fue encarcelado casi dos años en condiciones inmundas, mientras Ann arriesgaba su vida a diario para llevarle comida hasta que su propia salud falló y murió joven. Desde afuera parecía un fracaso. Pero en su hora más oscura Adoniram escribió: "el futuro es tan brillante como las promesas de Dios." Hoy más de cuatro millones de cristianos en Myanmar remontan su herencia a la fidelidad de los Judson.

blocks.en: 7. Walk by Faith, Not by Sight
blocks.es_reference: 7. Andar por Fe, No por Vista

blocks.en: Judson could not see the harvest in his lifetime, but he trusted the Lord of sight — and that is the heart of what Paul means when he writes, "we walk by faith, not by sight" (2 Corinthians 5:7). To walk by sight is to let only the visible, present evidence decide what we believe and how we act. To walk by faith is to let the promises of God decide, even when present reality makes those promises look impossible. Abraham did it leaving home; Judson did it in a Burmese prison; and God calls every disciple to it.
blocks.es_reference: Judson no pudo ver la cosecha en su vida, pero confió en el Señor de la vista — y ése es el corazón de lo que Pablo quiere decir cuando escribe: "andamos por fe, no por vista" (2 Corintios 5:7). Andar por vista es dejar que solo la evidencia visible y presente decida qué creemos y cómo actuamos. Andar por fe es dejar que las promesas de Dios decidan, aun cuando la realidad presente haga que esas promesas parezcan imposibles. Abraham lo hizo al dejar su hogar; Judson lo hizo en una prisión birmana; y Dios llama a todo discípulo a ello.

blocks.en: This means radical trust will regularly require us to step into obedience without seeing the whole map, and to keep trusting God's promises precisely when circumstances seem to contradict them. The line Judson clung to is worth carrying into every dark season: the future is as bright as the promises of God. Our feelings will often disagree, insisting the situation is hopeless — but faith does not take its orders from feelings. It looks past what is seen to the One who has spoken, and obeys.
blocks.es_reference: Esto significa que la confianza radical nos exigirá con regularidad entrar en la obediencia sin ver todo el mapa, y seguir confiando en las promesas de Dios justo cuando las circunstancias parecen contradecirlas. La frase a la que Judson se aferró vale la pena llevar a toda temporada oscura: el futuro es tan brillante como las promesas de Dios. Nuestros sentimientos a menudo discreparán, insistiendo en que la situación es desesperada — pero la fe no recibe órdenes de los sentimientos. Mira más allá de lo que se ve a Aquel que ha hablado, y obedece.

blocks.en: 8. Faith Over Feelings
blocks.es_reference: 8. La Fe Por Encima de los Sentimientos

blocks.en: Across all three of these movements runs a single thread: the choice of faith over feelings. In the boat, the disciples' feelings screamed that they were perishing, while the truth was that the Lord of the sea was with them. In the empty kitchen, feelings say there is no way, while the truth is that the Father knows our needs. In the dark prison, feelings say the mission has failed, while the truth is that God's promises are sure. Emotions are real, but they are not reliable guides; they report how things feel, not how things are.
blocks.es_reference: A través de los tres movimientos corre un solo hilo: la elección de la fe por encima de los sentimientos. En la barca, los sentimientos de los discípulos gritaban que perecían, mientras la verdad era que el Señor del mar estaba con ellos. En la cocina vacía, los sentimientos dicen que no hay salida, mientras la verdad es que el Padre conoce nuestras necesidades. En la prisión oscura, los sentimientos dicen que la misión ha fracasado, mientras la verdad es que las promesas de Dios son seguras. Las emociones son reales, pero no son guías confiables; reportan cómo se sienten las cosas, no cómo son.

blocks.en: So radical trust learns to act on what is true rather than on what is felt. When emotions say "fear," faith says "follow." This is not the denial of feeling — Jesus Himself was honest about anguish in Gethsemane — but the refusal to let feeling have the final word. We acknowledge the fear, and then choose to lean not on our own understanding but on the LORD with all our heart. The settled choice to trust, made again and again in small things, is what steadies us when the great storms come.
blocks.es_reference: Así que la confianza radical aprende a actuar sobre lo que es verdad en vez de sobre lo que se siente. Cuando las emociones dicen "miedo," la fe dice "sígueme." Esto no es la negación del sentimiento — el mismo Jesús fue honesto sobre la angustia en Getsemaní — sino la negativa a dejar que el sentimiento tenga la última palabra. Reconocemos el miedo, y luego elegimos estribar no en nuestra propia prudencia sino en Jehová de todo nuestro corazón. La decisión firme de confiar, hecha una y otra vez en cosas pequeñas, es lo que nos afirma cuando vienen las grandes tormentas.

blocks.en: 9. Where Do You Need Radical Trust?
blocks.es_reference: 9. ¿Dónde Necesitas Confianza Radical?

blocks.en: Radical trust is the stretching of new wineskins. The old way — fear, anxiety, self-reliance — bursts under the pressure of life's storms, but the new life Christ gives stretches us to hold faith. He is Lord over storms, and the wind and waves obey Him. He is Lord over worry, and your Father knows what you need. He is Lord of sight, and your future rests securely on His promises rather than on what you can presently see.
blocks.es_reference: La confianza radical es el estiramiento de los odres nuevos. La vieja manera — el miedo, la ansiedad, la autosuficiencia — revienta bajo la presión de las tormentas de la vida, pero la vida nueva que Cristo da nos estira para contener la fe. Él es Señor sobre las tormentas, y el viento y las olas le obedecen. Él es Señor sobre la preocupación, y tu Padre sabe lo que necesitas. Él es Señor de la vista, y tu futuro descansa con seguridad en sus promesas y no en lo que puedes ver al presente.

blocks.en: So the question comes to each of us personally. Where do you need radical trust today — in some storm that will not calm, in worries that steal your sleep, in a future you cannot make out? The Lord of the storm, of worry, and of sight is the same Lord, and He is calling you to stretch, to lean less on your own understanding and to trust Him more deeply. Trust in the LORD with all your heart; He has never once failed those who do, and the future before them is as bright as the promises of God.
blocks.es_reference: Así que la pregunta llega a cada uno de nosotros personalmente. ¿Dónde necesitas confianza radical hoy — en alguna tormenta que no se calma, en preocupaciones que te roban el sueño, en un futuro que no logras distinguir? El Señor de la tormenta, de la preocupación, y de la vista es el mismo Señor, y te está llamando a estirarte, a estribar menos en tu propia prudencia y a confiar en Él más hondamente. Fíate de Jehová de todo tu corazón; nunca una sola vez ha fallado a quienes lo hacen, y el futuro ante ellos es tan brillante como las promesas de Dios.

mc.stem: According to Proverbs 3:5-6, what are we told NOT to lean on?
mc.why: We are to trust the LORD with all our heart and lean not on our own understanding — letting go of the handrail of our own calculations to rest our weight on God.

mc.stem: How does the lesson use the wineskins image for trust?
options: The wine should be kept small
New wine expands; only new wineskins stretch to hold a faith beyond what feels safe
mc.why: New wine ferments and expands, bursting brittle old skins; new wineskins stretch. Jesus calls us to a faith that stretches beyond what feels safe — radical trust.

mc.stem: In Mark 4, where was Jesus during the violent storm, and what did He do?
options: Asleep in the stern; He rose and stilled the wind and waves with a word
Rowing the boat; He bailed water
mc.why: Jesus was asleep on a cushion in the stern; awakened, He rebuked the wind and said 'Peace, be still,' and the storm ceased — even wind and sea obey Him.

mc.stem: What is the central lesson of the calming of the storm?
options: Storms will never come to believers
The Lord of the storm is in the boat with you; His presence is greater than any wave
mc.why: The lesson is not that storms never come, but that the Lord of the storm is in the boat with you; radical trust knows His presence is greater than any wave.

mc.stem: How did Elisabeth Elliot demonstrate radical trust?
options: She went to live among the very tribe that killed her husband, and many came to faith
mc.why: Widowed at 29, Elisabeth trusted the Lord of the storm and went to live among the Huaorani who killed her husband; in time many — even some who held the spears — came to faith.

mc.stem: The lesson says faith rests on 'presence over outcome.' What does this mean?
options: God always gives the calm we ask for
Faith does not always stop the storm, but always anchors us to the Savior who rules it
mc.why: Elliot's storm was not calmed as she wished — her husband was not returned — yet Christ ruled over it; faith anchors us to the Savior even when the storm is not stopped.

mc.stem: In Matthew 6, to what does Jesus point to teach us not to worry?
options: The birds of the air and the lilies of the field, which the Father feeds and clothes
mc.why: Jesus points to birds that neither sow nor reap yet are fed, and lilies that neither toil nor spin yet outshine Solomon; if God so cares for them, how much more for us.

mc.stem: According to Jesus, what does worry actually accomplish?
options: Nothing — it cannot add a single hour to our lives
mc.why: Jesus asks who by worrying can add one cubit to his stature; worry accomplishes nothing and is a failure to reckon with the Father's care.

mc.stem: What is the antidote to worry that Jesus gives in Matthew 6:33?
options: Seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all these things will be added
mc.why: The antidote is to seek first God's kingdom and righteousness, trusting that the Father who knows our needs will add all these things; trust surrenders anxiety to Him.

mc.stem: The lesson contrasts 'what if?' with 'even if.' What is the point?
options: 'What if' is the language of faith
Anxiety asks 'what if?'; faith answers 'even if' — God is still faithful no matter the circumstance
mc.why: Anxiety multiplies 'what if?' fears that may never come; faith rests on 'even if' — even if the fridge is empty, God is faithful and knows what we need.

mc.stem: What daily disciplines of trust does the lesson recommend?
options: Worry productively and plan for every outcome
Surrender worries, seek first the kingdom, and thank God for provision before seeing it
mc.why: Surrender each worry to the Lord, seek first the kingdom over anxiety, and thank God for provision even before seeing it, for gratitude is faith remembering He never fails.

mc.stem: What does Hebrews 11:8 say about Abraham's obedience?
options: He went out, not knowing where he was going
He refused until he saw the land
He demanded a detailed plan first
mc.why: By faith Abraham obeyed and went out, not knowing where he was going — radical trust obeys before the map is clear, staking all on God's promise rather than sight.

mc.stem: What did Adoniram Judson endure, and what did he write in his darkest hour?
options: He gave up and went home
Years of slowness, prison, and loss; yet 'the future is as bright as the promises of God'
mc.why: Judson waited seven years for a convert, buried children, was imprisoned, and lost his wife; yet he wrote that the future is as bright as the promises of God.

mc.stem: What does 2 Corinthians 5:7 ('walk by faith, not by sight') mean in this lesson?
options: Let God's promises decide what we believe and do, even when present reality looks impossible
Only act on what you can see
Faith and sight are the same
mc.why: To walk by sight lets only visible evidence decide; to walk by faith lets God's promises decide, even when reality makes them look impossible — as Abraham and Judson did.

mc.stem: How does the lesson describe the relationship between faith and feelings?
options: Feelings are reliable guides to truth
We should always obey our feelings
Emotions report how things feel, not how they are; when feelings say 'fear,' faith says 'follow'
mc.why: Emotions are real but not reliable guides; they report how things feel, not how they are. Faith acts on truth — when feeling says 'fear,' faith says 'follow.'

mc.stem: Does walking by faith mean denying our emotions? How does the lesson answer?
options: No — Jesus was honest about anguish in Gethsemane; faith refuses to let feeling have the final word
Yes, all feeling must be suppressed
mc.why: It is not the denial of feeling — Jesus was honest about anguish in Gethsemane — but the refusal to let feeling have the final word; we acknowledge fear, then choose to trust.

mc.stem: The lesson names three things Jesus is Lord over. What are they?
options: Storms, worry, and sight (the unseen future)
mc.why: He is Lord over storms (wind and waves obey Him), over worry (the Father knows our needs), and of sight (our future rests on His promises).

mc.stem: What is the 'old way' that bursts under the pressure of life's storms?
mc.why: The old way — fear, anxiety, and self-reliance — bursts like a brittle wineskin under life's pressure; the new life in Christ stretches us to hold faith.

mc.stem: When the storm rises, what is radical trust's first instinct?
options: To pray first rather than panic first — turning to the One who commands the storm
mc.why: The first instinct of radical trust is to pray first rather than panic first, turning immediately to the One asleep in the stern who is Lord of wind and waves.

mc.stem: What closing question does the unit press on each believer?
options: Where do you need radical trust today — in a storm, in worries, or in an unseen future?
mc.why: The Lord of storms, worry, and sight is the same Lord, calling each of us to stretch — to lean less on our own understanding and trust Him more deeply.

fill.prompt: "Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and lean not on your own ____" (Proverbs 3:5).
Jesus rebuked the wind and said to the sea, "Peace, be ____!" (Mark 4:39).
The Lord of the storm is with us in the storm; faith is simply remembering who is in the ____.
Two years after her husband was killed, Elisabeth Elliot went to live among the ____ tribe that had killed him.
"But seek first the ____ of God and His righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you" (Matthew 6:33).
Anxiety speaks the language of "what if?"; faith answers in the language of "____."
By faith ____ obeyed when he was called, and he went out, not knowing where he was going (Hebrews 11:8).
In his darkest hour Adoniram Judson wrote, "the future is as bright as the ____ of God."
Paul writes, "we walk by faith, not by ____" (2 Corinthians 5:7).
Emotions are real, but they are not reliable ____; they report how things feel, not how things are.

sa.prompt: Explain Proverbs 3:5-6 and how the wineskins image frames radical trust.
sa.model: Proverbs tells us to trust in the LORD with all our heart and lean not on our own understanding, and in all our ways to acknowledge Him. We are to trust with all our heart, not a cautious portion, and specifically to stop leaning on our own understanding, which is the hard part because our understanding is exactly what we reach for when life turns frightening. When Jesus said no one pours new wine into old wineskins, He described the radical new life He brings: new wine ferments and expands, bursting brittle old skins, while new wineskins stretch to hold it. In the same way Jesus calls His disciples into a faith that stretches us beyond what feels safe or comfortable, a radical trust that does not collapse under storms, worries, or uncertainty, resting our whole weight on God rather than on our own calculations.

sa.prompt: Recount the calming of the storm (Mark 4) and state its central lesson.
sa.model: Jesus asked His disciples to cross the Sea of Galilee, and a violent storm broke out so fierce that the boat began filling with water. These were seasoned fishermen, yet the waves terrified them, and Jesus was asleep in the stern on a cushion. They woke Him crying, Teacher, do You not care that we are perishing? He rose, rebuked the wind, and said to the sea, Peace, be still, and there was a great calm, so that they whispered, Who can this be, that even the wind and the sea obey Him? The lesson is not that storms will never come, but that the Lord of the storm is in the boat with you, and His presence is greater than any wave. His question was not why the storm came but how is it you have no faith, for faith is simply remembering who is in the boat.

sa.prompt: How does Elisabeth Elliot's story illustrate trusting the Lord over storms?
sa.model: In 1956 five young missionaries were speared to death in Ecuador while trying to reach the Huaorani tribe, and Jim Elliot's wife Elisabeth, just twenty-nine with a baby daughter, was left a widow. She could have surrendered to bitterness and fear, but instead she trusted the Lord of the storm. Two years later she went to live among the very tribe that had killed her husband, showing them the love of Christ, and in time many Huaorani came to faith, including some of the men who had held the spears. Her story shows that radical trust does not depend on the storm being calmed the way we wish, for her husband was not returned to her, yet the same Jesus who stilled the Sea of Galilee ruled over her deeper storm and brought a harvest she could never have engineered.

sa.prompt: Explain 'presence over outcome' and why it corrects a shallow idea of trust.
sa.model: Elliot's story teaches what trust actually rests on, because her storm was never calmed in the way she might have wished and her husband was not given back. Yet the same Jesus who stilled the sea was unmistakably with her and ruled over the deeper storm. Faith does not always stop the storm; what it always does is anchor us to the Savior who rules over it. This corrects a shallow idea of trust, for we often assume that trusting God means He will give us the calm we ask for, the healing or rescue or restored situation. But the disciples' deepest need in the boat was not calmer water but to know who was with them. You may not be able to calm your storm, but you can rest in the One who commands it, so the first instinct of radical trust when the wind rises is to pray first rather than panic first.

sa.prompt: Explain how Matthew 6:25-34 teaches us to trust the Lord over worry.
sa.model: From the dramatic storm Jesus turns to the quiet daily storm of anxiety over food, drink, and clothing. He says do not worry about your life and points to the birds of the air, which neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, yet the heavenly Father feeds them, and to the lilies of the field, which neither toil nor spin, yet not even Solomon in all his glory was arrayed like one of them. If God so clothes the grass, will He not much more clothe us? Then He asks which of us by worrying can add a single hour or cubit to our lives, exposing worry as accomplishing nothing and failing to reckon with the Father's care. So He gives the antidote: seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all these things will be added. Radical trust surrenders anxiety to the Father who already knows exactly what we need before we ask.

sa.prompt: Explain the move from 'what if?' to 'even if,' using the testimony of provision.
sa.model: The practical shape of trusting God over worry is a change of vocabulary in the heart. Anxiety speaks the language of what if, asking what if the paycheck runs out, what if the diagnosis is bad, what if I cannot provide. Faith answers in the language of even if: even if the paycheck is small, even if the refrigerator is empty, even if the future is uncertain, God is still faithful and still knows what I need. Believers have testified to this in hard economic seasons. Picture a single mother in a deep recession, out of work, the fridge nearly empty, who breaks down one night and prays that though she does not know how they will eat, she trusts God; the next morning a friend from church arrives with bags of groceries, saying she felt God telling her of the need. Such testimonies make one point: God shows us we need not live in fear, because He knows what we need before we ask.

sa.prompt: Explain how Hebrews 11:8 and Abraham show trusting the Lord of sight.
sa.model: The third stretching of trust concerns the future we cannot see. Hebrews 11:8 tells us that by faith Abraham obeyed when he was called to go out to a place he would receive as an inheritance, and he went out not knowing where he was going. Romans 4 adds that he believed God's promise of a son even when his body and Sarah's were as good as dead. This is radical trust at its furthest reach: to obey before the map is clear and to stake everything on the promise of God rather than on the evidence of our eyes. The unseen future does not frighten such faith, because it rests not on what can presently be seen but on the One who has promised. Abraham did not need to see the land to leave for it; he needed only to trust the God who called him, and so he became the pattern of all who walk by faith into a future they cannot yet make out.

sa.prompt: How does Adoniram Judson illustrate walking by faith and not by sight?
sa.model: In 1812 Adoniram and Ann Judson sailed from Boston to Burma as among the first American missionaries, leaving family and security for a dangerous unknown. The work was agonizingly slow, with seven years passing before the first convert; disease struck repeatedly and they buried children; Adoniram was imprisoned nearly two years in filthy conditions while Ann risked her life daily to bring him food until her own health failed and she died young. From the outside it looked like failure. Yet in his darkest hour Adoniram wrote that the future is as bright as the promises of God. He could not see the harvest in his lifetime, but he trusted the Lord of sight, and today more than four million Christians in Myanmar trace their spiritual heritage to the Judsons' faithfulness, proving that to walk by faith is to let God's promises decide even when reality looks impossible.

sa.prompt: Explain the choice of faith over feelings that runs through all three movements.
sa.model: Across all three movements runs a single thread, the choice of faith over feelings. In the boat the disciples' feelings screamed that they were perishing, while the truth was that the Lord of the sea was with them. In the empty kitchen feelings say there is no way, while the truth is that the Father knows our needs. In the dark prison feelings say the mission has failed, while the truth is that God's promises are sure. Emotions are real but they are not reliable guides, for they report how things feel, not how things are. So radical trust learns to act on what is true rather than on what is felt, and when emotions say fear, faith says follow. This is not the denial of feeling, since Jesus Himself was honest about anguish in Gethsemane, but the refusal to let feeling have the final word; we acknowledge the fear and then choose to lean on the LORD with all our heart.

sa.prompt: Summarize the three lordships of radical trust and the question the unit presses.
sa.model: Radical trust is the stretching of new wineskins. The old way of fear, anxiety, and self-reliance bursts under the pressure of life's storms, but the new life Christ gives stretches us to hold faith. He is Lord over storms, and the wind and waves obey Him. He is Lord over worry, and the Father knows what we need. He is Lord of sight, and our future rests securely on His promises rather than on what we can presently see. So the question comes to each of us personally: where do we need radical trust today, in some storm that will not calm, in worries that steal our sleep, or in a future we cannot make out? The Lord of the storm, of worry, and of sight is the same Lord, calling us to stretch, to lean less on our own understanding and trust Him more deeply, for the future before those who trust Him is as bright as the promises of God.
